title: Why Do Planes Fly at 35,000 Feet?

thumbnail.plane: a stunned passenger pressed against an airplane window with wide eyes, a sea of clouds far below and a deep blue sky above, cinematic close-up, cold rim light
thumbnail.zoom: a cockpit altimeter dial reading thirty-five thousand feet, close-up, dramatic light

shots.vo: Right now, about seven miles above you, thousands of people are eating peanuts.
shots.prompt: an airliner cruising high above a sea of white clouds, deep blue sky, sun glinting on the wing, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Higher than Mount Everest. In air so thin you'd pass out in under a minute.
shots.prompt: the snowy summit of Mount Everest seen from above, an airliner contrail far higher in the dark blue sky
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: So why do planes go all the way up there? And why do eastbound and westbound flights use different heights?
shots.prompt: two airliners passing far apart at different heights above clouds at sunset, wide view
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Every flight does the same thing. Climb for twenty minutes, level off somewhere between thirty-one and forty-two thousand feet, then stay there.
shots.prompt: an airliner climbing steeply after takeoff over a city at dawn, landing gear up, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Climbing burns a huge amount of fuel. So it would be cheaper to stay low. Right?
shots.prompt: a jet engine at full power close-up with heat haze, dramatic light
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Wrong. Up there is where the plane is cheapest to fly.
shots.prompt: a calm airliner cabin at cruise, passengers relaxed, soft window light
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: The secret is the air itself. The higher you go, the thinner it gets.
shots.prompt: a view from high altitude where the sky fades from bright blue to dark navy at the top, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: At thirty-five thousand feet, the air is only about a third as thick as at the ground.
Thinner air means less drag. The plane slips through it, so the same fuel takes you much further.
shots.prompt: an airliner slicing cleanly through thin wisps of cloud at high altitude, motion, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Jet engines love it too. Air up there is around minus fifty degrees, and cold, dense intake air makes them more efficient.
shots.prompt: frost forming on the edge of an airplane wing at high altitude, icy blue light, close-up
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Then there's the weather. Almost all of it, the clouds, the rain, the storms, lives in the lowest layer of the sky.
shots.prompt: a towering thunderstorm cloud with lightning seen from the side, an airliner flying far above its top
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Its ceiling sits around thirty-six thousand feet. Fly near the top, and you're above most of the bumps.
Old propeller airliners couldn't get that high. They flew right through the weather, and passengers felt every storm.
shots.prompt: a 1950s propeller airliner bouncing through dark storm clouds, rain streaks, vintage painting style
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: But higher isn't always better. Go too high, and the air is too thin for the wings to hold you up at a safe speed.
shots.prompt: a lone airliner far above the clouds near the edge of space, the sky almost black, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Pilots call that squeeze the coffin corner. Too slow and the wing stalls. Too fast and it shakes itself apart.
shots.prompt: a tense pilot in a dim cockpit at night watching glowing instruments, close-up
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: So as a plane burns fuel and gets lighter, it climbs, step by step, to the height that's best for its weight.
shots.prompt: an airliner seen from below climbing gently into a bright blue sky, long contrail
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: And the different heights? That rule was written in blood. In 1956, two airliners collided over the Grand Canyon. A hundred and twenty-eight people died.
shots.prompt: the Grand Canyon at dusk seen from the air, somber light, wide view
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: It led to the creation of America's Federal Aviation Administration, and to strict rules for who flies where.
shots.prompt: a 1950s air traffic control room with radar screens and controllers, vintage photo style
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Today, flights heading east take odd thousands of feet, like thirty-five thousand. Flights heading west take even ones, like thirty-six thousand. They can never meet head on at the same height.
shots.prompt: two airliners passing in opposite directions with clear vertical separation above clouds, wide view, golden light
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Concorde flew at sixty thousand feet, where passengers could see the curve of the Earth. But for the rest of us, thirty-five thousand is the sweet spot.
shots.prompt: the curve of the Earth seen from very high altitude through an airplane window, dark sky above
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Thin air, cold engines, and a tragedy over the Grand Canyon. That's the hidden why.
shots.prompt: an airliner flying into a golden sunset above the clouds, peaceful, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark
